title: Puma Blue On Artistic Evolution And The Exorcism Of Performance
excerpt: From bedroom recordings to the collaborative experimentation of Croak Deluxe , Jacob Allen reflects on his changing relationship with songwriting, inspiration and live performance.
content:
Whether you delved into bedroom indie a decade ago, or you’ve more recently been exploring an ever-expanding international alt-R&B and jazz scene, you’ve almost definitely come across Puma Blue, a project by Jacob Allen. His first EP Swum Baby, featuring saxophone-dream hit ‘(She’s) Just A Phase’, became a sensual and simplistic cornerstone of how powerful a minimal track can be, and preceded several albums of sonic exploration. This year’s release Croak Dream, with its new instalment Croak Deluxe, hosts just as much sultry bass and vocals so gentle that they sound like they’re for your ears only. It pushes the boundaries of Puma Blue’s soundscape, his most genre-blending record to date, with electronic intervals layered over his trademark pristine instrumentation, and a through-line of lullaby-esque melodies.

Allen, managing to come across as thoughtful even over a constantly faltering WiFi connection, catches up with me in the midst of his European tour, having already trailed across the US. We discuss the creative process and its indeterminable source: ‘Music's become more of a spiritual practice for me. Ten years ago I still inherently felt something spiritual in the music, but I also thought I had a more powerful bearing over it than I do,’ he tells me. ‘Now I think music is something a lot bigger than me, and I'm a lot more grateful for it. When it comes to writing music now, I like to let inspiration find me working. I still show up, and practice guitar, but I also have more trust in the mystery of it, whereas it used to frustrate me.’

The artistic practice as an external force is a palpable blanket over Croak Deluxe in its thread of experimental sounds. This is particularly plain on ‘Untitled 1’, where spoken word, much like on Croak Dream’s ‘Mister Lost’, trails over indecipherable layers of gentle, grainy guitar and discordant echoes. It tells a story more abstract than it is elucidative, conjuring a dreaminess that offsets the harshness of the record as a whole. Both this song and the album as a whole are home to a form of play, a fantasy world that retains the soot of our reality. It’s the product of Allen’s symbiotic relationship with his craft, with music being something that he both creates and is created by.

‘You're definitely like a vessel for something much more magical, but at the same time, if I don't pick up the guitar, or practice my voice, or listen to music and try to make things that I find inspiring, the magic doesn't happen. I think you still have to meet it in the middle.’

Follow-up track ‘Still Jaded’ feels like the hazy echo of a club following you down the street as you depart onto the next bout of debauchery. It’s ominous and intoxicating, stemming from an evident adoration of the genres it combines. The whole album is an amalgamation of sounds and subcultures, homaging a scene that is at once ominous and comforting.

‘I was into embracing tougher sounds on this record. I was listening to a lot of krautrock-type music at the time, especially This Heat and Can. They've been a very important influence to me, on the Holy Waters album too. That kaleidoscopic hypnosis thing feels important to the way I write music for the band to play. I was also super into jungle and early dubstep whilst I was making this album. Producers like Photek, Muslimgauze, Bola, The Future Sound of London, Egoless, Mala, The Prodigy, Burial – the sonics of the rhythm, texture, grit – feel as ethereal to me as Jeff Buckley, in its own way.’

Trip-hop has been so explored and repackaged that it’s rare to hear such an entirely surprising approach to it as on Croak Deluxe. ‘Sweet Belief’ embodies this precisely; classic splippy breakbeating and dub elements blended with Puma Blue’s own trademark buzzy guitar tones and crooning vocals. The ongoing parallel of composition and performance creates an interesting process for the artist, where the reality of playing a track naturally informs its creation. This is part of the joy of working with a strong team of musicians, whose expression can be facilitated and teased out, Allen explains. ‘If I'm in a bass line, I'm trying to write something that Cameron [Dawson] from the band will enjoy playing, or I try to write a drum that I want to hear Ellis [Dupuy] play. Eventually, that's the way I'm going to be living with the song, in its live iteration. It takes me away from the bedroom band sound and more into writing stuff that gets our blood going.’

The heart-pumping deluxe closes on a few of these live performances, bringing the full circle to a state of resolution. An on-stage recording of ‘Croak Dream’ harmoniously balances clear vocals with a guttural bass and ghostly synths. It’s as exciting as the original lead single, professing the forward-moving momentum and integral spark of the record. ‘Desire’ is another track that impresses live, its immediately captivating drums cutting through the swampiness of the album’s other branches. There lies within it a passion for performance that can’t be feigned.

‘I just love it. I love it so much, getting to play. The guys that I tour with are some of my closest friends, and they have such spirit in their instruments. It's a true honour to get to play with them every night, and I really enjoy the exorcism of playing these songs. I also love the chaos, keeping it loose enough to improvise night to night, trying not to do the same thing twice. I love exploring the music.’

The evolution of Puma Blue’s sound is beautifully mappable, ramified from a solid core of origin in 2017 tracks like ‘Lust’ and ‘Moon Undah Water’. Croak Dream, with its tour closing and final tracks now released, is a bold, embodied record that consolidates the strength of this discography. It’s undeniably the kin of that early work, holding so much of its rawness and reverb, whilst demonstrating that the project has matured and progressed. Regardless of the shifts in sound and genre, Puma Blue’s music has an opacity and depth that allows its layers to endlessly unfurl. How these layers will reform in future work is yet to be seen, but will surely be just as enticing.
